answer.label: Not Winston Churchill — a later coinage credited to Abba Eban
answer.sourceLine: No Churchill source has been found for this line — not in any speech, letter, memoir, or writing. Quote Investigator credits the underlying aphorism to Israeli diplomat Abba Eban, who in 1967 said “nations do behave wisely once they have exhausted all other alternatives.” The specific “Americans … do the right thing” wording first surfaced in a 1970 U.S. Congressional hearing, and Churchill’s name was not attached until about 1980.

source.heading: The paper trail

docMeta.dd: U.S. Congressional hearing, 1970 (credited to an unnamed “Irishman”)

source.excerpt: “If I am sanguine on this point, it is because of a conviction that men and nations do behave wisely once they have exhausted all other alternatives.”
trail: Quote Investigator traces the earliest version to Abba Eban in 1967 and concludes the saying should be credited to Eban, not Churchill.
Churchill quotation expert Richard Langworth could find no solid attribution: “It cannot be found in any memoirs of his colleagues.”
The Hillsdale Churchill Project has been unable to locate the line in any transcript, memoir, speech, or correspondence.
source.excerptNote: Abba Eban’s 1967 formulation — the earliest documented version, per Quote Investigator. The familiar “Americans will always do the right thing” wording is a later paraphrase with no Churchill source.
source.rightsNote: The exact popular wording cannot be tied to any identifiable published work: it is an anonymous 20th-century paraphrase (first “Americans” form recorded in a 1970 hearing, credited to an unnamed speaker) built on Abba Eban’s 1967 spoken remarks. With no fixed source text or edition to point to, no copyright status can be honestly asserted.

author.name: Abba Eban
author.heading: About Abba Eban
author.bio: Abba Eban was an Israeli diplomat, politician, and celebrated orator who served as Israel’s Foreign Minister and ambassador to the United States and the United Nations. Renowned for his eloquence, he is the earliest figure Quote Investigator documents using the “behave wisely once they have exhausted all other alternatives” formulation — the seed of the saying later misattributed to Churchill.

misattribution.heading: How Churchill got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a classic case of what BBC quiz-host Nigel Rees named “Churchillian Drift” — a witty, quotable line drifting onto the most famous statesman available.

items.why: Churchill died in 1965, yet the earliest Churchill attribution is only about 1980. Per Quote Investigator, the evidence linking him to it is “late and very weak,” and no primary Churchill source contains it.
The earliest version — “nations do behave wisely once they have exhausted all other alternatives” — comes from Israeli diplomat Abba Eban in 1967, per Quote Investigator.
The first version naming “Americans” appears in a 1970 U.S. Congressional hearing, where it was ascribed to an unidentified “Irishman,” not to Churchill, per Quote Investigator.

misattribution.truthLine: No verified Churchill source has been found; the idea is Abba Eban’s (1967) and the “Americans” wording is an anonymous later paraphrase — Churchill-quotation editor Richard Langworth, writing for the Hillsdale Churchill Project, rates the evidence weak and the attribution unproven.

context.heading: Why it stuck to Churchill
lead: The line is a favorite of American politicians, who have quoted it on the House and Senate floor and in speeches for decades — almost always crediting Churchill. Its blend of affectionate insult and eventual optimism reads exactly like the Churchillian wit people expect, which is precisely why it attaches to him so readily.

But the paper trail runs the other way: the sentiment is first documented in the eloquent 1967 remarks of Abba Eban, was reshaped anonymously into its “Americans” form by 1970, and only acquired Churchill’s name around 1980 — fifteen years after his death.
context.pull: A quotable line drifts onto the most famous name available. Nigel Rees called it “Churchillian Drift.”
